t: The maskilim, as the movement's activists were called, sought to revive Hebrew as a language of secular literature, teach general subjects alongside Jewish ones, and bring Jews into the surrounding societies without ending Jewish distinctness.

The movement clashed with the traditionalist rabbinic elite, which wished to keep old Jewish values and norms in full, and also with radical assimilationists, whom the maskilim called pseudo-maskilim.

Historians once treated the Haskalah as the main cause of the changes in Jewish society, but later research narrowed its importance: state schools and new economic opportunities rivalled or overshadowed it, and in many regions it had no effect at all.
dyk: Abraham Mapu's Ahavat Zion, the first full-length Hebrew novel, was published in 1853 after twenty-three years of work.
ev: Moses Mendelssohn begins publishing Qohelet Musar, regarded as the first journal in Hebrew and the beginning of modern writing in the language
Maskilim help to found the Berlin Jewish Free School, the first institution among Ashkenazi Jews to teach general studies beside a reduced traditional curriculum
Hartwig Wessely circulates Divrei Shalom v'Emeth, calling on Jews to add science and the vernacular language to their children's curriculum
Isaac Abraham Euchel launches the quarterly Ha-Meassef in Königsberg, whose publishers call themselves Maskilim
Joseph Perl opens the first modern Jewish school in Galicia at Tarnopol
Joseph Perl publishes Megaleh Tmirin, a satire on Hasidic Judaism
Aleksander Zederbaum launches Ha-Melitz in Odessa, whose motto makes Haskalah the standard name of the movement
Pogroms in Imperial Russia lead many adherents of the Haskalah to turn towards proto-Zionist groups such as Hibbat Zion

f.where: Central and Eastern Europe, beginning in Berlin; later Vienna, Prague, Galicia, Vilnius, Warsaw and Odessa, the Pale of Settlement and Congress Poland; a certain influence in Western Europe and the Muslim world
f.period: arose as a defined worldview in the 1770s in Berlin; spread through Europe in the 19th century; its last stage ended at the close of the 19th century, after the 1881 pogroms in Imperial Russia
f.figures: Moses Mendelssohn, philosopher and translator of the Torah into German; Naphtali Hirz Wessely, poet and author of Words of Peace and Truth; Isaac Euchel, founder of Ha-Meassef; Joseph Perl, satirist and school founder; Isaac Baer Levinsohn, called the Russian Mendelssohn; Abraham Mapu, novelist; Judah Leib Gordon, poet; Aleksander Zederbaum, editor of Ha-Melitz
f.outcome: it revived Hebrew as a literary language and helped modernise education and culture among Central and Eastern European Jews, but its later historians judge its part limited; its adherents were divided, and after the 1881 pogroms many turned towards proto-Zionist groups
